mcqs.question: A tree-walking interpreter executes the same loop body a million times. What happens to the dispatch decisions made for each AST node inside that loop body?
options: They are recomputed from scratch on every single iteration, since nothing about a previous evaluation is remembered or reused
They are cached automatically after the first iteration
They are computed once when the AST is first built, not per iteration
They only need to be recomputed if the loop's condition changes
mcqs.explanation: Tree-walking has no mechanism to remember a previous evaluation's dispatch decisions, so the identical type-check-and-recurse work is redone in full on every single iteration — this is precisely the cost bytecode compilation exists to eliminate. There's no automatic caching, dispatch isn't decided at AST construction time, and the condition's value has no bearing on whether dispatch is recomputed.

mcqs.question: In a bytecode interpreter, when does the "what does this operation mean" dispatch decision actually get made?
options: Once, during compilation from the AST to bytecode — not repeated on each execution of that code
Once per execution of the bytecode, identical to tree-walking
Only when the program is about to terminate
Never — bytecode execution has no dispatch step at all
mcqs.explanation: The whole performance win comes from making that decision exactly once, up front, during compilation to bytecode, so repeated executions just replay cheap opcode dispatch instead of redoing the original decision. It is not repeated per execution (that would be no better than tree-walking), it isn't deferred to program termination, and bytecode execution absolutely still has a dispatch step — just a much cheaper one.

mcqs.question: In the `PUSH 2, PUSH 3, ADD` execution trace, what does the ADD instruction's handler actually do?
options: It multiplies the top two stack values instead of adding them
It reads two operands directly from the bytecode instruction's own encoded fields
It pops two values off the stack, adds them, and pushes the result back onto the stack
It recompiles the surrounding bytecode to fold the constants
mcqs.explanation: A stack-based VM's ADD pops its two operands from the shared stack (already pushed by the preceding PUSH instructions), adds them, and pushes the sum back — the stack itself carries the operands, not the instruction's own fields. It performs addition, not multiplication, and nothing about executing this instruction triggers recompilation.

mcqs.question: Why can a switch-based dispatch loop be slower than direct-threaded dispatch for the exact same bytecode?
options: Switch-based dispatch executes a different number of bytecode instructions than direct-threaded dispatch
A switch on the opcode is a data-dependent branch the CPU can mispredict on every dispatch, while direct-threaded code jumps straight to a pre-stored handler address with less branching overhead
Switch statements are only valid in interpreted languages, not in interpreter implementations
Direct-threaded code eliminates the need for an execution loop entirely
mcqs.explanation: Both techniques compute the same result and execute the same logical instructions; the difference is purely dispatch mechanics — a data-dependent switch branch is harder for the CPU to predict than jumping straight to a pre-stored handler address. Switch statements are ordinary code usable in any language implementing an interpreter, and direct-threaded code still needs a loop, just with cheaper dispatch inside it.

mcqs.question: A team says "we switched from tree-walking to bytecode, so we're now basically as fast as compiled native code." What's wrong with that claim?
options: Bytecode interpretation is not actually faster than tree-walking in any case

Bytecode interpretation still pays real per-instruction dispatch overhead on every execution — it's cheaper than tree-walking's dispatch, not eliminated the way JIT-compiled native code eliminates it entirely
Switching to bytecode requires abandoning the AST entirely, which is impossible
Native code and bytecode execute at identical speed by definition
mcqs.explanation: Bytecode is a real, worthwhile improvement over tree-walking, but it still runs an interpretation loop paying dispatch cost on every instruction — that gap only closes with JIT or ahead-of-time compilation to actual native instructions, which pay zero interpretation overhead. Bytecode genuinely is faster than tree-walking, the AST is still used during compilation to bytecode (not abandoned), and native code and bytecode are not the same performance tier.

mcqs.question: What's the single mechanical reason a bytecode VM outperforms directly walking the AST for the same program?
options: Bytecode VMs run on specialized hardware unavailable to tree-walking interpreters
The expensive work of understanding what code means and how to execute it happens once, during compilation to bytecode, instead of being redone on every single execution the way tree-walking does
Bytecode instructions are always shorter in total count than the equivalent AST has nodes
Tree-walking interpreters cannot execute loops at all
mcqs.explanation: The core mechanical difference is when the expensive dispatch/understanding work happens: once for bytecode, versus every single execution for tree-walking — that's the entire source of the speedup. No specialized hardware is involved, instruction count isn't the deciding factor, and tree-walking interpreters execute loops just fine, just slowly on each iteration.
